query: Which material can be used for lightweight and superior comprehensive performance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a systematic variation of aging temperature and duration to an as-fabricated Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high-entropy alloy (HEA) will refine the L21 precipitates, leading to enhanced yield strength and ductility while retaining a low density.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-fabricated Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high-entropy alloy exhibiting coarse or not fully optimized L21 precipitates.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical treatment via controlled aging, with systematic variation of temperature and duration.
generation.conditions: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures typical of aerospace or structural applications, without extreme high-temperature exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined L21 precipitate size and uniform distribution achieved through optimized aging parameters.
generation.mechanism: Fine-tuning the precipitate morphology (size, spacing, and volume fraction) via specific aging conditions impedes dislocation motion more effectively. This increases yield strength while maintaining ductility, thereby achieving a superior strength-to-weight ratio compared to the as-fabricated state.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy should exhibit enhanced mechanical performance—yield strength potentially exceeding 600 MPa coupled with improved ductility—while retaining its lightweight nature.
generation.baseline: Mechanical performance and precipitate morphology of the as-fabricated Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti HEA prior to any targeted aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The performance enhancements are expected under controlled aging conditions; however, if the aging temperature is too high or the duration too long, precipitate coarsening may occur, negatively affecting ductility and strength. The optimal parameters may also be sensitive to the specific service temperature range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal aging temperature and duration for achieving the ideal precipitate refinement are not yet established. Quantitative improvements in mechanical properties remain to be validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti HEA samples subjected to varying aging temperatures and durations. Characterize precipitate morphology using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and measure mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and density) through standard tensile tests. Compare the treated samples with the as-fabricated baseline. The experiment should span the range of aging conditions to identify the optimum and potential over-aging conditions.
measurements: TEM analysis for precipitate size, distribution, and phase identification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the aging treatments yield a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and ductility compared to the as-fabricated alloy, or if the treatments lead to coarsened precipitates that degrade mechanical performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] . decision.trend: Recent work on Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high-entropy alloys shows a shift toward integrating lightweight elements (Al, Ti) and leveraging precipitation (e.g., L21 phase) to achieve high strength and good ductility at reduced density. These alloys emerged from high-throughput computational screening, then were experimentally verified to maintain >600 MPa yield strength at elevated temperatures due to carefully engineered precipitates. Such precipitation-strengthening offers a path to performance levels comparable to heavier refractory or superalloys, yet with lower density.
decision.unsolved: While Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys demonstrate impressive strength-to-weight ratios, the detailed control of precipitate morphology, distribution, and stability across a broad temperature range remains an open challenge. Fine-tuning the aging steps or thermo-mechanical schedules to optimize nanoscale precipitates for further improving strength, ductility, and thermal stability has not been systematically resolved.
decision.lever: systematic variation of aging temperature and duration to refine L21 precipitate size and distribution
decision.why: Building on the demonstrated potential of precipitation-strengthened Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys, the logical next step is to enhance mechanical properties by optimizing the precipitation domain. Adjusting aging conditions can fine-tune precipitate size, spacing, and volume fraction, thus increasing strength and ductility without introducing new alloying elements.
